en: Thus have I heard: the Ghaṭikāra Sutta, the eighty-first discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya.
On one occasion the Blessed One was wandering on tour among the Kosalans together with a large community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, manifested a smile at a certain spot.
Thereupon, it occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What indeed is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having arranged his robe over one shoulder and extended his joined palms in reverential salutation toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Venerable sir, what is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile?
Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
“Once upon a time, Ānanda, in this very place there was a market town named Vegaḷiṅga, prosperous and flourishing, populous and crowded with people.”
“Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelt in dependence on the town of Vegaḷiṅga.
It was here, Ānanda, that the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was located.
It was here, Ānanda, that the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, while seated, exhorted the community of bhikkhus.”
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having spread out his outer robe folded fourfold, said this to the Blessed One:
“In that case, Bhante, let the Blessed One sit here.
This spot of ground will have been used by two Arhats, Perfectly Enlightened Ones.”
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“In the past, Ānanda, in this very place there was a market town named Vegaḷiṅga, prosperous, flourishing, populous, and crowded with people.”
Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelt in dependence upon the town of Vegaḷiṅga.
It was here, Ānanda, that the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was located;
it was here, Ānanda, that the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sat down and exhorted the community of monks.
"In the village and town of Vegaḷiṅga, Ānanda, there was a potter named Ghaṭīkāra who was the attendant and chief attendant of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Now, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla was a friend of the potter Ghaṭīkāra, a dear friend.
Then, Ānanda, the potter Ghaṭīkāra addressed the young brahmin Jotipāla:"
"Come, friend Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For it is my conviction that seeing that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is a good thing.
When this was said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
‘Enough, friend Ghaṭīkāra.
What is the use of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?
A second time, Ānanda, [he said the same]...pe...
A third time, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the young man Jotipāla:
“Come, dear Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For it is considered excellent by me to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
A third time, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“Enough, friend Ghaṭīkāra!
What is the use of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?”
“In that case, my dear Jotipāla, let us take our bathing cloths and go to the river to bathe.
“Very well, sir,” the young brahmin Jotipāla replied to Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter and the young brahmin Jotipāla took their bathing cloths and went to the river to bathe.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter addressed the young man Jotipāla:
“Friend Jotipāla, here is the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not far from here.
Come, friend Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
‘For it is highly esteemed by me to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
When this was said, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
‘Enough, friend Ghaṭīkāra.’
"But what is the use of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?
A second time, Ānanda...
and a third time, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the young man Jotipāla:
“Friend Jotipāla, here is the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not far from here.
Come, friend Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
for it is held by me that seeing that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is a good thing.”
A third time, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“Enough, friend Ghaṭīkāra!
What is the use of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?”
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter, having grasped Jotipāla the young brahmin by the wrist, said this:
“My dear Jotipāla, here is the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not far away.
Come, my dear Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.”
‘For it is highly esteemed by the virtuous to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla rolled up his turban and said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
‘Enough, friend Ghaṭīkāra.’
“But what is the use of seeing that shaven-headed ascetic?
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter, having rubbed the head of the young man Jotipāla who had washed his hair, said this:
“Friend Jotipāla, here is the monastery of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, not far from here.”
"Come, friend Jotipāla, let us go to see the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
For it is held by me to be a good thing to see that Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Then, Ānanda, this thought occurred to the young brahmin Jotipāla:
‘It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
That this potter Ghaṭīkāra, though being of low birth, should think himself worthy to touch the hair of us who have bathed our heads;
surely, I do not think this can be something insignificant.’
He said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“Is it as much as that, friend Ghaṭīkāra?
“It is as much as that, friend Jotipāla.”
"For indeed, it is my considered view that it is good to see that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"In that case, friend Ghaṭīkāra, let go; we shall go.
Then, Ānanda, the potter Ghaṭīkāra and the young brahmin Jotipāla went to where the Blessed One Kassapa was.

They approached the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Ghaṭīkāra the potter sat down to one side.
But the young brahmin Jotipāla exchanged greetings with the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One. After exchanging courteous and friendly greetings...
Having exchanged courteous greetings, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, this young brahmin Jotipāla was my friend, my dear companion.”
"May the Blessed One teach him the Dhamma.

Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened Ghaṭīkāra the potter and Jotipāla the young brahmin with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter and Jotipāla the young brahmin [listened] to the Blessed One Kassapa...
Instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by the Dhamma talk of the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
they rejoiced and expressed their appreciation for what was spoken by the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One; then, rising from their seats,
they paid homage to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, circumambulated him with their right side toward him, and departed.
Then, Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla said this to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“Friend Ghaṭīkāra, having heard this Dhamma, will you still not go forth from the home life into homelessness?
“Do you not know me, friend Jotipāla? I am supporting my blind and aged mother and father.”
‘In that case, my dear Ghaṭikāra, I shall go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Then, Ānanda, Ghaṭikāra the potter and the young brahmin Jotipāla approached the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One;
having approached, [they paid homage to] the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant...

Having paid homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Ānanda, Ghaṭīkāra the potter said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, this young brahmin Jotipāla was my friend, my dear companion.”
"May the Blessed One grant him the going-forth.
Ānanda, the young brahmin Jotipāla received the going-forth in the presence of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One; he received full ordination.

Then, Ānanda, after the young brahmin Jotipāla had been ordained for not long—having been ordained for half a month—the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having stayed at Vebhaḷiṅga as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Bārāṇasī.
Wandering by stages on his journey, he arrived at Bārāṇasī.
There, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, was staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.

Then, Ānanda, Kikī, the King of Kāsī, heard: “The Blessed One Kassapa, it is said, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has arrived at Bārāṇasī and is staying at Bārāṇasī in the Deer Park at Isipatana.”
Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsī had fine carriages harnessed;
mounting a fine carriage and accompanied by fine carriages, he set out from Bārāṇasī with great royal splendor to see the Blessed One Kassapa,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having traveled by carriage as far as the ground would permit for a carriage, he alighted from the carriage and approached the Blessed One Kassapa,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, on foot. Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One Kassapa,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and sat down to one side.

As Kikī, the King of Kāsi, sat to one side, Kassapa— the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One— instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma. Then, Ānanda, having been instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened by Kassapa,
the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, with that discourse on the Dhamma, Kikī, the King of Kāsi, [addressed] the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant...
He said this to the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal tomorrow, together with the community of monks.
Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, consented by remaining silent.
Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsī, understanding the Blessed One Kassapa’s acceptance,
rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and keeping him to his right,
departed. Then, Ānanda, at the end of that night, King Kikī of Kāsī, in his own residence, prepared exquisite solid food...

Having had food prepared—fine rice from which the black grains had been removed, along with many soups and many curries—he announced the time to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready.”
Then, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
dressed in the morning and taking his bowl and robe, went to the residence of King Kikī of Kāsī; having arrived,
he sat down on the prepared seat together with the community of bhikkhus.
Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsī, with his own hands, satisfied and served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with excellent hard foods and soft foods.
Then, Ānanda, when the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, King Kikī of Kāsī took a certain low seat,
sat down to one side, and said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One consent to my invitation for the rains residence at Bārāṇasī;
such will be the service to the Saṅgha.
“Enough, great king.”
"I have accepted the rains-residence.
A second time, Ānanda...
and a third time, Ānanda, Kikī, the King of Kāsī, said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept from me a rains residence at Bārāṇasī;
such will be the service for the Saṅgha.
“Enough, great king.”
"I have accepted the invitation for the rains retreat.

Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsi felt a sense of dejection and sorrow, thinking, "The Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has not accepted my invitation for the rains retreat in Bārāṇasī.
Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsi said this to the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One:
“Venerable sir, is there indeed anyone else who attends upon me more than I do?
“There is, great king. There is a market town called Vebhaḷiṅga.
There, a potter named Ghaṭīkāra lives.”
"He is my attendant, my chief attendant.

But for you, Great King, there is indeed a change of state and there is sorrow because the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, does not accept your invitation to spend the rains retreat in Bārāṇasī;
whereas for Ghaṭīkāra the potter, there is neither [change of state] nor will there be."
"Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra has gone for refuge to the Buddha, he has gone for refuge to the Dhamma, and he has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha.

Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra abstains from taking life, abstains from taking what is not given, abstains from sexual misconduct, abstains from false speech, and abstains from fermented liquor, spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence."

“Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra possesses unwavering confidence in the Buddha, unwavering confidence in the Dhamma, and unwavering confidence in the Saṅgha; he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones.

Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra is free from doubt regarding suffering, free from doubt regarding the origin of suffering, free from doubt regarding the cessation of suffering, and free from doubt regarding the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.”
"Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter eats but one meal a day; he is celibate, virtuous, and of noble character.
Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter has laid aside gems and gold; he is free from bullion and silver.
Great King, Ghaṭikāra the potter uses a wooden pestle; he does not dig the earth with his own hands."
Whatever rubble from the riverbank or mouse-droppings there were, he would bring them home on a carrying-pole, fashion them into vessels, and say:
"Whoever wishes may place here bags of rice, bags of mung beans, or bags of peas, and take away whatever they desire.
Great King, the potter Ghaṭīkāra supports his blind and aged mother and father.

"Great King, the potter Ghaṭikāra, through the complete destruction of the five lower fetters, was one of spontaneous birth, destined to attain final nibbāna there, not subject to returning from that world.
Once, Great King, I was staying at a market town named Vebhaḷiṅga.
Then, Great King, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I went to where Ghaṭikāra..."
We approached the parents of Ghaṭīkāra the potter and, having approached them, we said this to the parents of Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
"Well now, Bhaggava, where has he gone?"
“Venerable sir, your attendant has gone out; please take rice from the inner pot and sauce from the side dish-tray and eat.
Then, Great King, having taken rice from the pot and sauce from the side dish-tray and eaten, I rose from my seat and departed.
Then, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached his parents; having approached them, he said this to his parents:
“Who was it that took rice from the pot, took curry from the side-dish, and having eaten, rose from his seat and departed?

“It was the Blessed One Kassapa, dear father, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, who took rice from the pot, took curry from the side-dish, and having eaten, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, Great King, this occurred to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“It is a gain for me indeed, it is a great blessing for me indeed,
that the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
has placed such confidence in me. Then, Great King, for half a month the joy and happiness did not leave Ghaṭīkāra the potter, and for seven days they did not leave his parents.
"Once, Great King, on a certain occasion, I was staying right there at the town of Vebhaliṅga.
Then, Great King, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I went to where Ghaṭīkāra the potter’s mother and father were; having approached, [I went] to Ghaṭīkāra the potter’s..."
His parents said this:
"Well now, Bhaggava, where has he gone?
"Venerable sirs, your attendant has gone out; having taken some boiled rice from the pot and some curry from the saucepan, he is eating it."
Then, Great King, having taken the rice from the basket and the curry from the bowl, I ate and rose from my seat and departed.
Then, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached his parents; having approached, he said this to them:
"Who was it that took the rice from the basket and the curry from the bowl, ate them, and then rose from his seat and departed?"

“Dear Kassapa, the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having taken the rice-porridge from the basket and the curry from the bowl, ate it and then rose from his seat and departed.
Then, Great King, it occurred to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“It is indeed a gain for me! It is truly well-obtained by me!”
“Because the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, has thus commended me.
Then, Great King, for half a month the joy and happiness did not leave Ghaṭīkāra the potter, and for seven days it did not leave his parents.
On one occasion, Great King, I was dwelling right there in that market town named Vebhaḷiṅga.
Now at that time, the hut was leaking.
Then, Great King, I addressed the bhikkhus:
“Go, bhikkhus, and find some grass at the house of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.”
When this was said, Great King, those bhikkhus said to me:
“Venerable sir, there is no grass in the potter Ghaṭīkāra’s dwelling, but there is a thatched roof over his workshop.
“Go, bhikkhus, and clear the grass from the potter Ghaṭīkāra’s workshop,” I said.
Then, Great King, those monks thatched the workshop of Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Then, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter’s parents said this to those monks:
“Who is thatching the workshop?”
“Bhikkhus, sisters, the hut of the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is leaking.
“Take it away, venerable sirs! Take it away, good sirs!
Then, Great King, Ghaṭīkāra the potter approached his parents; having approached them, he said this to his parents:
“Who has had my workshop thatched?
“It was the monks, dear father, because the hut of the Blessed One Kassapa—the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One—is leaking.
Then, Great King, it occurred to Ghaṭīkāra the potter:
“It is indeed a gain for me, it is truly well-gained by me,
that the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One,
has placed such confidence in me. Then, Great King, the joy and happiness did not leave Ghaṭīkāra the potter for half a month, nor for seven days his mother and father.
"Then, Great King, for the entire three months, the workshop stood with its roof open to the sky, and it did not rain.
Such, Great King, was Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
"It is a gain, Bhante, for Ghaṭīkāra the potter; it is a great fortune, Bhante, for Ghaṭīkāra the potter."
“...to whom the Blessed One has thus entrusted himself.
Then, Ānanda, King Kikī of Kāsī sent five hundred cartloads of fine rice from the *paṇḍu* variety, along with suitable curry, for Ghaṭīkāra the potter.
Then, Ānanda, those royal messengers approached Ghaṭīkāra the potter and said this:
“Venerable sir, these five hundred cartloads of *pāṇḍu-puṭaka* rice and its accompanying curry have been sent by Kiki, the King of Kāsi.
Venerable sir, please accept them.
“The king, indeed, has many duties and much to do.”
‘Enough for me;
let it belong to the king alone.
Now, Ānanda, it may occur to you thus:
‘Could it be that at that time Jotipāla the young brahmin was someone else?
‘It should not be seen thus, Ānanda.
At that time, I myself was Jotipāla the young brahmin.’
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The First Discourse on Ghaṭikāra is concluded.
